text: Monte Carlo prediction Core idea: follow the policy for complete episodes and average the returns that actually followed each state.
label: core
key: the return actually observed to the end of the episode

text: The value is literally the mean return, so by the law of large numbers the estimate converges to V π ( s ) as the number of visits grows ( Silver, Lecture 4 slides ).
label: core
key: by the law of large numbers

text: Run an episode with policy π until it terminates.
label: fat

text: Walk backwards through it computing each return, G t = R t +1 + γ G t +1 with G T = 0.
label: core

text: For each visited state, move its estimate towards the return that followed it.
label: fat

text: First-visit MC uses only the first visit to a state in each episode; every-visit MC uses every visit.
label: depth

text: First-visit returns are independent, identically distributed samples of V π ( s ), so each average is unbiased and its error's standard deviation falls as 1/√ n in the number of returns n ; every-visit MC is harder to analyse (several returns from one episode are correlated, and its estimate is biased for a finite number of episodes), but it also converges, and it "extends more naturally to function approximation and eligibility traces" ( Sutton and Barto, §5.1 ; the comparison is Singh and Sutton 1996 , who also tie first-visit MC to replacing traces and every-visit MC to accumulating ones).
label: depth

text: The running average can be kept incrementally, because a mean satisfies μ k = μ k −1 + (1/ k )( x k − μ k −1 ), where μ k is the mean of the first k samples x 1 , ..., x k .
label: depth

text: Replacing 1/ k by a constant step size gives constant-α MC , which forgets old episodes and so tracks a changing (non-stationary) problem: V ( S t ) ← V ( S t ) + α ( G t − V ( S t ) ) V(S t ) the current estimate for the state visited at time t G t the return actually observed from time t to the end of the episode α the step size (1/ N ( S t ), with N ( S t ) the visit count, gives the exact running mean) G t − V(S t ) the error the update shrinks Properties: Unbiased : G t is a sample of exactly the quantity V π ( S t ) is the expectation of.
label: core

text: High variance : G t depends on every random action, transition and reward until the end of the episode.
label: core
key: carries every random action, transition and reward to the end

text: Needs episodes that terminate : the target is unknown until the episode ends, so MC only applies to episodic tasks and learns nothing mid-episode.
label: core

text: No bootstrapping : the estimate of one state does not build on the estimate of any other, so the cost of estimating one state does not depend on the number of states; you can generate episodes from the states you care about and ignore the rest ( Sutton and Barto, §5.1 ).
label: depth

text: It does not rely on the Markov property, so it copes better when the state does not capture everything that matters ( Silver, Lecture 4 slides ).
label: core
key: not used: better when the state is partly observed

text: History: the term "Monte Carlo" dates from the 1940s at Los Alamos; an early use to estimate action values in RL was Michie and Chambers (1968), who averaged episode durations in pole balancing, "similar in spirit to Monte Carlo ES with every-visit MC estimates"; Monte Carlo ES itself first appeared in the 1998 edition of Sutton and Barto ( chapter 5 notes ).

text: After one step, you know one real reward and where you landed, and you already have an estimate of how good that place is.

label: core
